Notre Dame is truly helping me grow as a whole person by getting me closer to great people and nurturing positive values in my soul. It takes people with the curiosity to question established ways of thinking, the courage to test new ideas and the persistence to turn possibilities into reality. That mindset is exactly what I encounter every day at FOSS - and what keeps us looking for what's next.

publications.subtitle: ICCV Workshop: Vision Foundation Models and Generative AI for Accessibility
publications.description: (Oral Presentation) Building upon our COREVQA work, applying it to those who are visually impaired. Visual Entailment is an essential skill allowing researchers to assess visual understanding. Through this paper, we address the real-world implications of assistive technology like BeMyEyes, and how they struggle in real-world scenarios. We propose a path towards better assistive technology software.

publications.title: COREVQA: A Crowd Observation and Reasoning Entailment Visual Question Answering Benchmark
publications.subtitle: ICML Workshop: Data in Generative Models
publications.description: Recently, many benchmarks and datasets have been developed to evaluate Vision-Language Models (VLMs) using visual question answering (VQA) pairs, and models have shown significant accuracy improvements. However, these benchmarks rarely test the model's ability to accurately complete visual entailment, for instance, accepting or refuting a hypothesis based on the image. To address this, we propose COREVQA (Crowd Observations and Reasoning Entailment), a benchmark of 5608 image and synthetically generated true/false statement pairs, with images derived from the CrowdHuman dataset, to provoke visual entailment reasoning on challenging crowded images. Our results show that even the top-performing VLMs achieve accuracy below 80%, with other models performing substantially worse (39.98%-69.95%). This significant performance gap reveals key limitations in VLMs' ability to reason over certain types of image-question pairs in crowded scenes.

This past Friday, I officially wrapped up my summer as a Software Engineering Intern on Cisco's Industrial IoT team in San Jose! Over the past few months, I worked on Agentic Runbook Creator (ARC) for Cisco's AI Assistant for Troubleshooting Networks. Runbooks are step-by-step diagnostic scripts used to troubleshoot industrial networks automatically, and ARC is used to generate said runbooks dynamically using context from a customer's network. My work included connecting local SLM-based hypothesis generation with cloud LLM workflows and protecting sensitive topology and device data during the handoff between on-premises and cloud activity. I also directly developed a cloud-based digital-twin evaluator that injects IOS-XE simulated faults into the customer's obfuscated topology to test whether the generated runbooks actually work. Ultimately, we brought estimated network downtime for new faults from hours to ~25 minutes, and expanded runbook coverage beyond 13 preexisting implementations! Working on ARC gave me a much better understanding of what it takes to build AI for real systems. The output needs the right context, and the workflow has to protect customer data from the start. The whole system also needs to hold up when tested against realistic failures. Taking the project from separate components to a connected workflow taught me a lot about integration and iteration, while working on an engineering team showed me how much I can learn from asking questions and listening to feedback. Everyone told me to avoid my TA. She was "scary"... She taught me more than anyone this summer. That's Arvie Violette . She TA'd my program at Stanford SIMR. The reputation was real to be honest. High standards, always asked the follow-up question you were praying she'd skip. Giving that season one Jessica Pearson vibe. Most people avoid that person. They drift toward whoever seems friendliest. I almost did the same thing. Here's what I'd have missed. When people find out you're 17, the conversation quietly changes. They simplify. They praise stuff that isn't good. They stop correcting you. It feels great. That's the problem. You walk around thinking you understand things you don't. Arvie never did that, not once. She'd let me be wrong, explain exactly why, then expect me to keep up. Warm the whole time. She just never lowered the bar. A few things I'd pass on if you're in a program like this: Ask the question you actually have, not the one that sounds appropriate for your level. "I don't get why that term is there" will ALWAYS get you further than nodding. Be wrong out loud. In front of someone with real standards that's the fastest way to learn anything. In front of someone who's just impressed you showed up, it costs you nothing, which is exactly why it teaches you nothing. And go talk to the intimidating one. I know it's the opposite of what feels good. Arvie, thank you. You made the science make sense and the hard weeks survivable. CGEN NeuroSync: Closed-Loop BCI for Instant Workspace Adaptation I'm incredibly excited to announce the public release of CGEN NeuroSync. If you are a developer, creator, or technical builder, you know how exhausting "The Prompting Tax" is, the constant, manual context-switching and UI coordination required to get digital help tools to cooperate. CGEN NeuroSync completely eliminates that blockage. By utilizing a non-invasive, closed-loop Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), our system translates neural intent into instant workspace execution. Essentially, no manual prompting and no workflow lag. To make this seamless, I engineered a dual-agent framework that achieves an unprecedented sub 50ms edge processing latency: 1. Agent Synapse: Real-time biological noise/muscle artifact filtering and continuous calibration. 2. Agent CGEN: The dynamic UI/UX workspace adaptation engine. Watch the full video here to see the full architectural breakdown: https://lnkd.in/g3AHQMt5 LIVE Website - running full-stack pipeline (Fast API + JS) and streaming real-time visualizations: https://lnkd.in/gRFpWYxv ...more

Most engineering frameworks treat hardware, Artificial Intelligence, and biology as completely separate departments. However, the biggest breakthroughs over the next decade will happen exclusively at their intersection. To prove it, I spent the last few months digging into the history, methodologies, and emerging trends of cross-modal engineering. Today, I’m excited to officially share my research paper: "EE&Innovation". In this work, I break down: - The Convergence: How Electrical Engineering serves as the foundational architecture bridging biomedical telemetry and modern AI systems. - Historical Paradigms: What past hardware constraints can teach us about optimizing current resource-heavy deep-tech models. - Future Trends: Why the future of innovation belongs to interdisciplinary polymaths building at the absolute baseline of physical and digital systems. Whether you're building deep tech, researching neural architectures, or scaling hardware, I'd love to get your eyes on this and hear your feedback. This week, Dex turns two. Great timing to humblebrag about our Q4, but I wouldn't. Instead, I'd share the struggles of building a non-census company as a group of parents. A few days ago, Charlie and I had a co-founder heart-to-heart. I walked him to BART, and he was shaking in the SF wind. “Why?” I asked. “Last week the whole family was sick, right when we’re fast-following the subscription launch. That week really got me,” Charlie replied, and sighed. All of a sudden, guilt took over. His wife told me—half-jokingly—that Charlie wakes up every day at 3:30AM and sneaks out like a thief into the home office. Sometimes their daughter wakes up and asks, “What time is it, Dad? Where are you going?” Charlie slips away as if he didn’t hear. I laughed and lightheartedly told Charlie to take it easy. But I felt guilty. Our lives run like clockwork: wake up, work, parenting, work, parenting, sleep. 7 days a week. 52 weeks a year. Every kid’s sick day is a major boss fight. Every weekend feels like a juggling act because we can’t unplug from work or parenting. And as the CEO, I felt bad. Dex is a hard business, and I sorta got everyone (mostly parents themselves) into this mission impossible. Think about it… we’re trying to create the canonical children’s technology—AI, software, content, devices, EVERYTHING—by a team of 8 FTE in a sardine office, with $5M in funding. Every hour matters. Every dollar matters. We want scale. We also want profitability. We want speed. We also want quality. In Q4, we magically got all of those. Then I realized: we also want each employee to be happy, and their families well taken care of. How can I have it all, continuously? Fundraising and hiring? Deep down, I know Dex is an underdog company. We need to achieve so much to convince the “mainstream”/“playbooked” investors. So I don't want to waste time until we're undeniably exceptional. Be less ambitious? I consider Dex the work of my life. I’d rather reach for the vision and fail than not try. Parent less? No way. Unfair for our children. Unfair for our better halves. So the truth is, I don’t know how to have it all. What I do know is: tomorrow, I’ll live to fight another day—to defend our vision, take care of the team, and be a good parent. Gladly, those struggles come with a bright side. When I’m stretched thin, I think about my Ironman races. In the last leg, each step felt like hell. But each step also gave me that rush: I’m reaching a point I’ve never reached before. Building Dex is like racing an Ironman, but with a mission. Each day of relentless work is a testament to our vision. Just like every early morning, late night, and weekend of showing up to our children is a testament to our love for them. If you made this far: thank you. This was personal. I hope it gives you a little energy, too. ...more ...more

Excited to be a launch partner for Baseten Labs! We believe that the future is multi-model (and multi-modal). That's why we're partnering with Baseten to bring agentic search to every dataset. People often misinterpret "The Bitter Lesson": It's about using general methods, not about creating general models. AlphaGo (it's prime example) is the opposite of general (it only plays Go) but was trained using general methods. There is value to general models, but often this generality comes at the cost of outright performance. So what you really want to maximize is leverage on computation. At SID.ai , we have found ways to get much more leverage for the task of search. We expect many other tasks to go this way. The future will be multi-model not as a compromise to save money, but because specialized models are simply better: faster, cheaper, and more accurate at the thing you actually need. Unlike Go, search is very useful. We’re thrilled to partner with Baseten to bring this utility to everyone. Together we offer agentic search at 20x lower latency and 100x lower cost than a general frontier model, at equal or better accuracy. As always: reach out if you want to chat & we're hiring!

Two years ago, I joined DramaBox to build something that didn't exist yet: a US content production studio for vertical short drama, from the ground up. Today, I'm closing that chapter, and I'm carrying so much with me. We built a team from scratch and a methodology that connected development, production, and market strategy into one loop. When I arrived, content and growth barely spoke to each other. By the end, every project was a full-cycle conversation between them. We produced at a scale and hit rate I'm deeply proud of. We spearheaded our Disney Accelerator journey and the partnership that grew from it. And we went beyond making shows, partnering with Cal State LA to teach the next generation of filmmakers how to make microdrama, and helping build the creative ecosystem this format needs to last. But the thing I'll carry most is the people. This team trusted me, built alongside me, and cared about the work in a way that made all of it possible. Thank you. I'll be cheering you on always. So, what's next? I'm thrilled to share that I've joined Pocket FM as AVP, Head of Content. Here's the bet I'm making. I believe the next year in this industry belongs to retention. The last few years were about acquisition, everyone competing to pull users in. But as that gets more expensive and attention more fragmented, the winners will be the ones who can actually keep people. And that comes down to one thing: content worth coming back to. I also think AI is about to change the shape of storytelling in a way most people aren't expecting. As production cost collapses, the constraint on length disappears, and I believe content trends longer, deeper, and more immersive, not shorter. Pocket FM has been building exactly that in audio: stories people return to for hundreds of hours. That's a future I want to help shape. New medium, new challenge. I'm here to learn, and I'm here to build. If you're working on the future of content, AI storytelling, or audio, let's connect.

A facilities team can know exactly which building needs attention and still fail to secure funding from the Board. Not because the project is unimportant. Because the people holding the purse need a different level of proof. They need to know: What will this investment change? What will it cost? How confident should we be in the outcome? When budgets are tight, a facilities proposal cannot stop at “the HVAC system is aging” or “this building is using too much energy.” Those facts matter, but they are not yet a capital plan. A stronger proposal starts with the building’s operating history: Utility costs. Meter trends. Equipment runtime. Maintenance history. Weather, schedules, and occupancy. Then it compares the choices. Repair or replace. Optimize controls or phase an upgrade. Add solar or continue buying power from the grid. The goal is to show what each option changes, what it costs, and what risks remain. This is where Edviro helps. We connect bills, meters, building systems, schedules, and capital planning tools so facilities and finance teams can compare capital scenarios with the same evidence. The work can only begin when the person approving the budget can see why the project matters. What evidence has helped your facilities team get a capital project approved?

Your MD’s comment takes ten seconds. Getting the page can take hours. You already know what is wrong with the page. Saying it is the easy part. projects.title: VeriFi
projects.description: VeriFi — A C++ and React RAG chatbot that grounds answers in verified policy documents Product Owner & Vector Store Engineer · 5-person Agile team · Live demoCustomer-facing chatbots hallucinate on dense policy questions — a regulatory and financial liability — and keyword search doesn't help, since it matches strings, not meaning. VeriFi constrains an LLM to answer only from passages retrieved at query time from verified Fidelity Investments policy documents, citing the document and page behind every claim.Offline, a Python pipeline extracts layout-aware text from PDFs with PyMuPDF, chunks it semantically, and embeds each chunk into a 384-dim vector via Sentence Transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) — 580 chunks, 59 pages. Per query, the question is embedded the same way, the C++ store ranks every chunk by cosine similarity and returns the top-K, and those passages plus a grounding prompt go to gpt-4o-mini. The React UI shows citations and match scores.My contribution: I owned the vector store — the core retrieval engine — and built it from scratch in C++17 rather than reaching for Pinecone or FAISS. I implemented the in-memory store and its load_from_jsonl parser (nlohmann/json), cosine similarity from its primitives (dot product, magnitude), and the O(N) brute-force k-NN search() with descending-score ranking. I added dimension and empty-input guardrails that fail loudly instead of returning silently wrong matches, property-based tests for self-retrieval correctness, and a benchmark harness measuring load and search throughput, then exposed the store to Python via a JSON-over-stdio CLI the FastAPI backend drives as a subprocess.As Product Owner: set scope, wrote the architecture docs, reviewed and merged every PR, ran the release across four sprints, and built the GitHub Actions workflow deploying the demo to GitHub Pages.Stack: C++17 · Python · FastAPI · Sentence Transformers · OpenAI API · React 19 · TypeScript · Vite · pytest · GitHub Actions

projects.title: NVPilot
projects.description: NVPilot is like personalized medicine for your PC. Just as a doctor doesn't prescribe the same treatment to every patient, NVPilot doesn't apply the same settings to every machine — it reads your specific hardware, figures out what's actually holding your system back, and applies exactly the optimizations your machine needs for whatever you're running.Instead of nerfing your graphics like a one-size-fits-all preset, it identifies which settings are genuinely costing you performance on your GPU specifically, changes only those, and leaves everything else at full quality. It reasons about your whole system together — background apps eating your RAM, process priority, power plans, and game configs — rather than tuning each in isolation, so every optimization accounts for what's actually happening elsewhere on your machine.

projects.title: Neural-Inference-Engine
projects.description: This project is about understanding how neural network inference actually works — not by calling into a library, but by implementing the forward pass myself in C++.I train a small MNIST MLP in PyTorch (784 → 128 → 64 → 10), export the learned weights to a flat binary format, then run inference in a hand-written C++ engine with no ML libraries at runtime. That means owning the core pieces end to end: matrix multiply, bias add, ReLU, and argmax, plus loading the PyTorch-exported weights into the network.The goal isn’t just “get MNIST working.” It’s to build a clear path from training → weight export → CPU inference, prove the C++ engine matches the PyTorch baseline numerically, and then optimize for real performance (SIMD, multithreading) with a CUDA port planned after the CPU path is validated.Right now, training/export and the C++ forward path (including weight loading) are in place and unit-tested; the next milestone is sample-level validation against PyTorch on the full test set.

publications.title: Inferring Agenda: An Unsupervised Approach to SCOTUS Issue Classification
publications.subtitle: The Ohio State University
publications.description: This project presents an end-to-end machine learning pipeline to process, embed, and cluster large-scale legal text data, addressing computational efficiency and interpretability challenges present in high-dimensional natural language data. The goal is to analyze judicial behavior at the petition stage of the U.S. Supreme Court by classifying legal texts into issue areas based on the SPAETH Supreme Court database, a widely used dataset that codes Supreme Court decisions by various characteristics, including legal issue area. A key limitation, though, is that only accepted petitions are labeled with a SPAETH category. To understand the topic distribution among all petitions, consensus clustering was employed on the full set of petitions to infer clusters that approximate SPAETH issue areas. This was preferable over supervised learning because supervised methods would rely on training a classifier on accepted petitions and then applying it on unaccepted petitions; however, this strategy would introduce a sampling bias because the training sample would not be random. We can use the resulting clusters to determine the semantic content of a petition, thus enabling us to compare what the Supreme Court is asked to hear vs. what they actually hear. The Supreme Court can unilaterally strip and provide rights to people, but, until now, the factors regarding case selection were a mystery. This research offers a data-driven framework to provide critical insights into whose voices are amplified, whose are silenced, and how the Supreme Court steers national policy.

Exciting news. We're No. 1251 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list! But the number isn't the story. We grew because of the problem we're solving and how we're solving it. The story is what happens to your resume after you hit submit. It doesn't usually get rejected. Rejection would be a response - and I know from my many job searches, a response is sometimes too much to ask:(. Instead the resume gets uploaded to an S3 bucket in a data center in Northern Virginia. Encrypted at rest. Replicated across three availability zones. Amazon guarantees it eleven nines of durability (Azure is probably similar), which means your resume is statistically more likely to survive the next century than most governments (dependent on data retention policies:)). What a journey your lonely resume gets to be a part of. It is safe. It is indexed. It is beautifully preserved. It has simply never been read by a person. That's not cruelty. That's one person with 400 applications and nine days. And all the tools do is match words on pieces of digital paper (four clusters generally matched between resume and JD). We fixed the silence. We allowed our customers to talk to and interview all candidates in real-time. Finding the best fit NOW, while building pipeline for the next role. Thank you to our customers, our partners, and the team that built this while I was busy writing Linkedin posts. Congrats to everyone else on the list. Aiming for the top 500 next year! Everyone is using AI to code, but most developers are still spending hours reviewing the output and reprompting models to fix the same minor issues over and over again. The biggest gain with AI should not just be generating code faster; it should be drastically reducing the time you spend reviewing it before anything ships. That’s why we built Agentic IDE Inc. Instead of catching the same problems in review every sprint, our infrastructure encodes the rules for how things get implemented before your agent ever starts working, so you get quality code the first time rather than spending hours undoing what AI introduced. Today we are launching Plan Mode, and here is a look at what is making this possible: Containerized Knowledge Profiles allow you to swap knowledge layers in under 30 seconds using automatic skills backed by semantic, relational, and graph storage that accurately model human reasoning across your entire codebase. Skill Audits Prior to Execution mean that before your agent writes a single line of code, our harness automatically finds and injects your team's most relevant rules into context, catching things like silent retries where it should fail hard before they ever make it into review. Autonomous Agent Fleets connect to a shared brain profile to take on parallel jobs simultaneously, letting your team execute complex tasks at a speed that simply was not possible before. Nobody has built a production-quality gate for AI harnesses until now, and we want to help teams stop reviewing AI slop and start shipping code they can actually stand behind. If you are ready to cut your refactor and review time by hours, try Plan Mode at aideapp.dev and reach out if you want to bring it to your team.

A food delivery app is only as good as the people behind every order. Before an order gets to a customer in perfect condition, there’s a lot that happens behind the scenes to make that possible. - From the vendors preparing and packaging every meal. - The riders who brave the sun and the rain to deliver it. - And the customers who trust us with their orders. Every delivery is made possible by people. We believe those stories deserve to be told because stories help us see the people behind the service. They remind us that behind every order is someone working hard to make someone else’s day a little easier. That’s why we created People Who Swoop—a series that shines a light on the people who make Swoop what it is. Every episode tells the story of the people behind the brand, why they do what they do, and gives us all the opportunity to see the job from a different perspective. Our first episode follows Idris, one of our top-performing riders, through a typical day on the road. We also had a little surprise waiting for him at the end. 💜

But growing up as the shortest, weakest, and shyest person among my peers, I learned that who I am does not define what I do. “You can’t play sports because you’re short.” “You can’t speak in public because you’re shy.” “You can’t lead because you’re awkward.” I believe the second half of every one of those statements. But not the first. Not because I want to prove anything, but because what I want to pursue simply isn’t what I’m naturally good at. And that’s okay. There is wisdom in playing to my strengths, but I choose to believe in the courage it takes not to back down from my weaknesses.

Swoop just raised $7.3 million to launch food delivery in Yaba. But the food delivery is almost beside the point. The actual bet is this: if you can get a Lagos user to open your app every time they want lunch, you've built something more valuable than a delivery business. You've built a daily habit. And a user with a daily habit is a user you can eventually ask to send money, buy airtime, pay bills, without having to earn their trust from scratch each time. That's the super app thesis. Food delivery as the opening move. Financial services as the destination. It's a sound idea. It's also the same idea that OPay, Gokada, and MAX all had at different points, and all eventually stepped back from, because the distance between "user who orders food" and "user who trusts you with their money" is longer and harder to close than the thesis assumes. The retention problem inside the super app model is specific. Food delivery builds frequency, but frequency alone doesn't build financial trust. A user can order from Swoop three times a week and still open a different app when they need to transfer money, because the mental category for "food app" and "money app" doesn't automatically collapse just because they live in the same interface. What closes that gap is something Chowdeck has been building quietly for four years, the kind of reliability that makes a user stop thinking about whether the app will work and just use it. That's not something $7.3 million buys directly. It accumulates through consistent delivery, through rider networks that hold up in the rain, through customer service that resolves the order that went wrong. Swoop is starting in Yaba, which is a sensible choice. Dense restaurants, users who already order online, infrastructure that's manageable. But Yaba is also where Chowdeck, Glovo, and FoodCourt already operate. The users Swoop actually needs to convert to make the super app thesis work, lower-income, cash-preferring, first-time digital consumers on the outskirts of Lagos, are not in Yaba. And those users are going to require a very different activation and trust-building approach than the ones already comfortable ordering food on their phones. Whether the habit Swoop builds in Yaba is the right foundation for the product they actually want to become is the question worth watching. Do you think food delivery can genuinely build the kind of daily trust that makes a Lagos user move their money through the same app, or does financial trust have to be earned on its own terms?

projects.title: Comparing Convolutional Neural Network Strategies to Label Tricuspid Valve on MRI Images of the Heart
projects.description: Project aimed to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of heart failure diagnosis by automating the labeling of MRI images using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The study trained, tested, and validated CNNs on 9,960 MRI images to identify key points of the tricuspid valve: the centroid, the ends of the valves, or a combination of both. Models were evaluated based on their accuracy using Euclidean distance measurements. Demonstrates the potential of CNNs to automate and standardize MRI image labeling, offering a cost-effective solution that can save time and improve the diagnostic process for heart conditions.

This past Friday, I officially wrapped up my summer as a Software Engineering Intern on Cisco's Industrial IoT team in San Jose! Over the past few months, I worked on Agentic Runbook Creator (ARC) for Cisco's AI Assistant for Troubleshooting Networks. Runbooks are step-by-step diagnostic scripts used to troubleshoot industrial networks automatically, and ARC is used to generate said runbooks dynamically using context from a customer's network. My work included connecting local SLM-based hypothesis generation with cloud LLM workflows and protecting sensitive topology and device data during the handoff between on-premises and cloud activity. I also directly developed a cloud-based digital-twin evaluator that injects IOS-XE simulated faults into the customer's obfuscated topology to test whether the generated runbooks actually work. Ultimately, we brought estimated network downtime for new faults from hours to ~25 minutes, and expanded runbook coverage beyond 13 preexisting implementations! Working on ARC gave me a much better understanding of what it takes to build AI for real systems. The output needs the right context, and the workflow has to protect customer data from the start. The whole system also needs to hold up when tested against realistic failures. Taking the project from separate components to a connected workflow taught me a lot about integration and iteration, while working on an engineering team showed me how much I can learn from asking questions and listening to feedback. Adoption is binary, skill is a spectrum, and your tracker only measures the binary. Train your top slice and give them somewhere to publish. publications.title: Enabling Lifelong Learning in AI with Biologically-inspired Neural Networks Based on Short-Term, Working, and Long-Term Memory
publications.subtitle: IEEE Computer Society
publications.description: Achieving lifelong learning, the ability of a learning system to continuously acquire and adapt to changing data, in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is crucial to achieving Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a hypothetical, human-like version of AI that has endless possibilities in various domains. Currently, the vast majority of models are incapable of exhibiting lifelong learning because they demonstrate catastrophic forgetting. This research theorizes the first Neural Network architecture based on combining the Three-stage Memory Model, Working Memory Model, and Complementary Learning Systems (CLS) Theory, key theories on our brain’s cognitive processes, to overcome catastrophic forgetting. By developing a complementary learning architecture comprising the Cerebral Cortex, Prefrontal Cortex, and Hippocampus, mimicking Long-term, Working, and Short-term memory, respectively, this research achieves lifelong learning on the CLEAR benchmark and an artificial form of lifelong learning on the CIFAR dataset. This research also proved the favorability of using combined principles of the Three-stage Memory Model, Working Memory Model, and CLS theory to further achieve human-like cognition in AI. To support that, experiments revealed that the complementary learning nature of the architecture creates an unexpected learning phenomenon and pattern of machine "reasoning" that increases accuracy. Therefore, this research reveals this architecture as a possible way of further achieving human-like cognition in AI, and consequently a pathway to add to the body of research in achieving AGI one day.

publications.title: Enabling Lifelong Learning in AI with Biological Neural Networks Based on Short-Term, Working, and Long-Term Memory
publications.subtitle: 8th Annual Conference on Cognitive Computational Neuroscience
publications.description: Achieving Lifelong Learning, the ability of a learning system to continuously acquire and adapt to changing data over time, in Artificial Intelligence (AI) is an integral step towards achieving Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a hypothetical version of AI that can change our world forever. Currently, the vast majority of models are incapable of exhibiting Lifelong Learning. This research theorizes the first Neural Network architecture inspired by the Three-stage Memory Model--a theory on our brain's memory. By developing a complementary Neural Network learning system comprising the Cerebral Cortex, Prefrontal Cortex, and Hippocampus, mimicking Long-term, Working, and Short-term memory, respectively, this research achieves Lifelong Learning on a simulated computer vision task and develops the first Working memory-inspired model. It also demonstrates the feasibility of using the Three-stage Memory Model for achieving human-like cognition in AI. Therefore, this research reveals a pathway for future research in achieving AGI: the Three-stage Memory Model.

publications.title: Resolving Gender Biases in LLMs at Inference Time with Novel Dijkstra’s-based K-Explorers Neural Network Traversal (KeNNT)
publications.subtitle: Association of Computational Linguistics
publications.description: The vast growth of Large Language Models (LLMs) has increased the need for larger data corpora, and researchers often turn to the internet for a source of that data. However, with rising online sexism, LLMs start to pick up on gender biases in the text they generate. Despite protective measures, biases still infiltrate newer models like ChatGPT and LLaMA 2. In this research, we introduce a novel Dijkstra’s-based algorithm called K-explorers Neural Network Traversal (KeNNT), that we hypothesize can be attached to models and algorithms to solve optimization problems. KeNNT is a novel method to guide Transformer models away from generating gender biases. KeNNT, based on Dijkstra’s shortest path algorithm, was tested on a GPT-2 model fine-tuned on the WinoBias benchmark dataset. KeNNT reduced gender bias in generated texts by 84.79% (K = 3) and 95.93% (K = 4), outperforming some industry standards. Based on the promising results, it is hypothesized that KeNNT can enhance other optimization algorithms, such as Gradient Descent, improving accuracy and avoiding local minima convergence. With this work, we hope to inspire further, novel endeavors into gender bias resolution and new perspectives on optimization problems.

activity.title: We had a serious security incident last month. Not going to get into the specifics, but it was something most teams building agents have already hit. It made something click for us: API keys are treated like a minor inconvenience if they leak, but for AI they're closer to a blank check. A leaked credit card number costs someone a few hundred bucks. But a leaked API key to a model provider can cost someone a lot, fast, because every company is already burning serious spend on inference. The labs don't have great monitoring for this yet. Some are building it now, mostly reactively, following their own incidents. So we shipped an open source red-teaming tool. Point your agent's endpoint at it, we run an audit, and you get a concrete proof of concept of where your agent is actually exposed. We're dogfooding this internally too. If you're building agents in production, this is worth taking seriously to avoid an unpleasant surprise. ...more

I don't think AEO is a separate discipline yet. Google has a mature, well-understood algorithm. You can study it, reverse-engineer patterns, and build a playbook that works for your company. AI search engines don't expose anything like that. So anyone doing aeo right now is mostly guessing at an algorithm nobody's shown them. I'd rather keep doing seo well, because the fundamentals carry over regardless of who's reading it, be it a human or a model. SEO used to take about 6 months to show results. People expect leads in three months now. Well, it's still not going to spike in a week. And traffic isn't the win condition. We built a thousand landing pages once and got a ton of traffic. But then we had to figure out why that traffic wasn't converting. ...more

Besides our zip code, moving to SF for YC also changed the ceiling on what we thought we were allowed to build. Our original plan was to move back to Illinois once the batch ended, but that never happened. When we were still in Illinois, we were just students. We knew the basic rule: build something people actually want. But the only people around us were other college students, so that's exactly what we built - a job search platform, sized to the world we could see from campus. Within a week or two of arriving here, the plan to "spend a few months here, then move back to Illinois" was dead. We went to events constantly, met founders every week, and a surprising number of them became friends (some eventually became customers). We'd run into people from companies like Stripe and Azure at almost every event, and they'd walk us through credits and product details we never would have found sitting in a dorm room. Looking back, I don't think our instinct back in Illinois was wrong. Plenty of great companies get built for a local community first. But the scale of what you believe is possible tends to mirror the scale of what you see around you every day. Surrounded by students, we built for students. And once we were surrounded by people trying to build global companies, we started to believe we had a fair shot at it, too. ...more ...more

We ran the company on $500k for two years and still had $200,000 left in the bank when we decided to raise. And we grew close to 600% last year before closing our seed round. Speed and closeness to customers did most of the work. We talked to customers constantly, asking for feedback directly instead of guessing. That closeness let us iterate on the product fast enough to earn word-of-mouth. We never spent a dollar on marketing or ads. A meaningful amount of our growth came from other YC founders recommending us to each other. There's a WhatsApp group of YC founders, and in a typical week, 2-3 of them would recommend us to someone else without us ever asking them. We also got a lot of intros and platform credits through the broader YC network, often through customers who'd point us toward the right people. We didn't engineer any of this. It came from spending two years staying frugal and trying to build a product good enough for other founders to vouch for it themselves. When you're not spending on acquisition, the product and the relationships have to do the heavy lifting, so you gotta make sure they actually can.

Excited to announce that my team and I took 2nd place at the Amazon Intern Hackathon! Early in the summer I got blocked on my own project for a while. Different root cause, but the feeling stuck with me: knowing exactly what you want to build and losing days to figuring out who can unblock you. Then I started hearing the same thing from interns across completely different orgs. Who owns this package. Why can't I access this. Everyone had a workaround, nobody had an answer, and every one of them assumed it was just their team's quirk. It wasn't. When the same friction shows up independently across that many teams, it stops being a people problem and becomes a systems problem. That's the kind worth building for. So when the theme came out as "Pay It Forward," we already knew what we were solving. We built Path. Under the hood, it's a knowledge map of who owns what, who can approve what, and how code actually moves to prod. You type a question the way you'd ask a coworker, and instead of a search results page you get a short list of names, ranked by who can actually unblock you, each one linked to their profile. The answer is a person, not a doc. The hard part wasn't building the map. It was cutting everything that wasn't the map. We scrapped features the night before demos and the product got sharper every time. Shoutout to my teammates Andrew Lin , Ava Martoma , and Jacob Ryabinky . I've never seen a team disagree that productively at 1 am. Huge thanks to Emma Hanan , Betty Beniam , and the rest of the AFE team who put this amazing event together!

Thrilled to share that my team and I just took 2nd place at the Amazon AFE Hackathon! Working internally at Amazon this summer has given me a firsthand look at how massive the organizational structure can be, especially for a new employee. Inspired by this year's theme of "Pay It Forward," we built Path, an evidence-backed knowledge graph designed to help new engineers and interns "find their path from Day One." Ask a normal question in plain English -- "Who owns this package?" or "Can I edit this in prod?" -- and Path traces the real ownership, access, and deployment paths across teams, packages, pipelines, and accounts. It then returns a ranked list of exactly who to reach out to, with a link straight to their internal Amazon profile. A huge thank you to my incredible teammates Daniel Lee , Jacob Ryabinky , and Andrew Lin for the amazing teamwork. Thank you also to Betty Beniam , Emma Hanan , and everyone who helped make the hackathon happen. Looking forward to more great work! #Amazon #Hackathon #PayItForward #Innovation

As I wrap up my summer as an Engineering Intern at Swagelok , I want to take a moment to reflect on an incredible experience. Coming into my first engineering internship, I was excited to learn and grow while seeing how my project scope sheets turn into fully implemented systems on the manufacturing floor. These last several months have done all of that and more. I had the opportunity to work on projects that challenged me technically, developed my leadership and communication skills, and gave me a new point of view on manufacturing operations. From my first day doing orientation at the Distribution Center, to the Summer in The Land Guardians game, to being the captain of the winning Cleveland Corporate Challenge Arcade Basketball team, to giving my final presentation. Every moment here has been an opportunity for me to succeed, and I couldn't appreciate it more. My supervisors Trent Babcock and Dean Peska have been nothing but supportive throughout the entire summer and with their guidance I've been able to work on meaningful projects that allowed me to take ownership for projects I never would've imagined receiving as an intern. For my first project, huge thanks to my project sponsor Micheal Zickes for working with me on this, I was given a project focused on digitizing production reports. I developed VBA macros for production documentation with integrated barcode scanning, improved validation logic, and PDF generation to improve efficiency, data security, and customer ease of use. I was able to work with operators to refine this form to their liking and decrease the time taken to complete these forms from when it was completed manually by around 80% (roughly 2 minutes 30 seconds to roughly 30 seconds) with a decrease in errors in the form to 0% because of the increased data security. For my second project, another massive thank you to my technical sponsor Micheal Duplay for all of your assistance, I was assigned to support updates on a vision system workstation. For this project, I was able to learn how to use Studio 5000 and FactoryTalk View to update code with new instructions on a process logic controller (PLC) and new images on a human machine interface (HMI) to help make part assembly more efficient. This gave me a massive insight into the future of manufacturing and what controls engineers do on a daily basis. The team and I were successfully able to get the vision system updated and it is now up and running at an improved capacity! Beyond the technical work, one of the most valuable parts of this internship was getting to meet wonderful people all across Swagelok. Through networking 1:1s, Lunch and Learn's, and facility tours, I was able to gain a deeper understanding of how the business operates from manufacturing all the way to sales, and all of the departments in between that keep everything running like a well-oiled machine. Thank you, Swagelok, for an unforgettable summer. Looking forward to what's next. #AdventureAwaits

activity.title: This past weekend, Adam Zeineldin , Reyan Yousif , Bassil Shalaby , and I built Immortal at Anthropic’s Hackathon and won Best Healthcare Hack. We were frustrated that wearables collect tons of health data but don’t actually help you do anything with it. You can see your HRV drop, but not why, what to change, or how to test it. So we built a closed-loop system that learns your personal baselines, detects meaningful changes, and turns them into evidence-backed recommendations with real citations. The part we’re most excited about is self-experiments. You can test something like cutting caffeine after 2pm, and Immortal will track the before and after, compute the effect, and tell you if it actually worked. We paired deterministic models for reliability with an LLM layer for personalized guidance, which ended up being a really strong combination. We built Circa a smart farming management system designed to tackle one of agriculture's most persistent problems: inefficient irrigation. The turret's design extends circular irrigation to rectangular fields, meaning less wasted space and far more precise water delivery. Apparently startup founders are getting older. This is terrible news. Who is going to keep the hoodie industry alive? Ever since dot-com we've been sold the image of the successful founder as a 23-year-old living on ramen, fueled by energy drinks and venture capital. The research says otherwise. When you look at the fastest-growing startups, the average founder is about 45 years old. Not 25. Forty-five. And honestly... that matches exactly what I see in Seattle. The average founder in the Venture Mechanics Catapult Accelerator is over 45, married with children. Many are "second-career" entrepreneurs who just left Microsoft, Amazon, Boeing, or another large company with something even more valuable than a severance package: 20-30 years of domain expertise. They're building AI infrastructure, enterprise software, robotics, aerospace, defense, climate tech, healthcare, and industrial systems—the kinds of companies where experience compounds instead of depreciates. Turns out spending a couple of decades learning how an industry is broken is pretty good preparation for fixing it. Maybe that's why the stereotype has it backwards. Your 20s are for learning. Your 30s are for mastering. Your 40s are when you finally know which problems are actually worth solving. So if you're in your 40s or 50s wondering whether you missed your chance to build a startup... ...you may have just aged into your competitive advantage. One question for the 40+ crowd: If your resume and your severance package were your seed round... what would you build?

🛰️ Meet Circa — a precision irrigation platform powered by K2 Think V2 that lets any grower, in any language, apply true precision watering to their fields. Why focus on farming? Agriculture accounts for roughly 70% of global freshwater use. Circular irrigation saves water compared to traditional rectangular methods, but leaves the land in the corners underused. Circa’s hardware addresses both: a directional turret with full X/Y/Z control, paired with moisture-sensing nodes that tell the system exactly where and when water is needed. The result is irrigation that responds to what the soil actually needs, not a fixed schedule. The software layer handles live sensor data, manual targeting, automated sweeps, and ML-powered soil moisture forecasts — with an AI assistant powered by K2 Think V2 at its center. Farmers do not need to learn a complex interface to water their crops. Using K2 Think V2, the Circa team lets each grower describe what they want in plain language; the model parses intent, extracts parameters (zone, threshold, duration), and creates live automation rules the system executes. What makes this stand out: ✨ Natural-language rule creation that executes directly — no interface learning curve. ✨ Live soil moisture sensing with ML-powered forecasting from distributed field nodes. ✨ Multilingual input designed in, not bolted on. I'm not a fan of deep learning. At least the one I see most commonly. Real Deep Learning is the kind pioneered by people who deeply understand optimisation, geometry, and why gradients behave the way they do. However, the deep learning most people practice is one where they scale up a network, throw more data at it, and hope the loss goes down. That's not engineering. That's prayer with GPUs (and thanks to you why Nvidia nearly has a $5T market cap). I'm much more on the inductive bias side. Classical ML, carefully chosen priors, models that actually reflect what you know about the data. Your dataset is almost never as big as you think it is, and the structure you encode is the structure you don't have to learn from scratch. The uncomfortable truth is that model choice is often the least interesting decision in the stack. If your data is bad, no architecture saves you. If your data is good, a linear model often gets 90% of the way there and most people never bother to look. The best DL paper I've read recently is LeJEPA by Yann LeCun and collaborators. Real maths. Real priors. Not a single mention of "just add more layers." That's the deep learning I have time for the kind where the architecture means something. Garbage in, garbage out. Generative garbage in, generative garbage out. Agentic garbage in... well, you get the idea. ...more ...more

publications.title: An Exploratory Study of Single Channel Surface Electromyography for Hand Gesture Classification
publications.subtitle: Minnesota Undergraduate Research & Academic Journal
publications.description: Accurate hand gesture recognition using surface electromyography (sEMG) typically relies on multichannel sensor arrays and computationally intensive models. This limits practical deployment in low-power and embedded systems. This study investigates the feasibility of classifying ten hand gestures using a single sEMG channel combined with lightweight machine learning architectures. Raw sEMG signals were transformed into a comprehensive feature-based representation, including time-domain, frequency-domain, higher-order-crossing, and relative-intensity features. Feature redundancy was reduced using Pearson correlation filtering and the removal of highly correlated features, while dimensionality-reduction techniques (LDA and PCA) were applied selectively. Three classifiers, a feed-forward neural network (NN), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and a support vector machine (SVM), were systematically evaluated across four experiments. Results demonstrate that combining time and frequency features with Pearson filtering and a compact NN can achieve up to 90 percent accuracy, even with limited temporal and spatial information. These findings highlight the potential of single-channel sEMG systems for cost-effective, low-power gesture-recognition applications.

publications.subtitle: MINNESOTA UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH & ACADEMIC JOURNAL
publications.description: This study explores the application of machine learning models, specifically a pretrained ResNet-50 model and a general SqueezeNet model, in diagnosing tuberculosis (TB) using chest X-ray images. TB, a persistent infectious disease affecting humanity for millennia, poses challenges in diagnosis, especially in resource-limited settings. Traditional methods, such as sputum smear microscopy and culture, are inefficient, prompting the exploration of advanced technologies like deep learning and computer vision.The study utilized a dataset from Kaggle, consisting of 4,200 chest X-rays, to develop and compare the performance of the two machine learning models. Preprocessing involved data splitting, augmentation, and resizing to enhance training efficiency. Evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and confusion matrix, were employed to assess model performance. Results showcase that the SqueezeNet achieved a loss of 32%, accuracy of 89%, precision of 98%, recall of 80%, and an F1 score of 87%. In contrast, the ResNet-50 model exhibited a loss of 54%, accuracy of 73%, precision of 88%, recall of 52%, and an F1 score of 65%. This study emphasizes the potential of machine learning in TB detection and possible implications for early identification and treatment initiation. The possibility of integrating such models into mobile devices expands their utility in areas lacking TB detection resources. However, despite promising results, the need for continued development of faster, smaller, and more accurate TB detection models remains crucial in contributing to the global efforts in combating TB.

We built a senior HVAC technician that fits in your earbuds. On-device by default. Works without a signal. You see every time it reaches out. Shipped this weekend at the Gemma 4 Voice Agents Hackathon at YC SF (Cactus × Google DeepMind × Y Combinator). The judging panel included @Andrew Miklas (YC GP). The US is short ~110,000 HVAC technicians. Training a new one takes 3-5 years. Experienced techs close jobs on the first visit far more often than juniors. So we put a senior tech on a chip. The build: Gemma 4 E4B via @Cactus (YC S25) on an M4 MacBook Pro. Three clients, one runtime: Chrome, iPhone Safari, and Rokid Corporation Ltd AR glasses over WebRTC. Audio + vision + function calling in ONE forward pass. No Whisper → ViT → LLM stitching. 6 HVAC tools. 5 on-device + 1 explicit online-escalation with a UI banner. You can see every time it hits the network. The gnarliest engineering problem: Gemma 4 emits three different tool-call opener syntaxes within the same model. Parens, pipes, and a mid-pipe-missing curly form. Raw markers were leaking into every transcript. Built a stateful token sanitizer that buffers partial markers off the wire and emits clean suffixes. Users see clean text. The tool-loop still captures structured calls. Numbers: 217 ms bare-model TTFT, 17 tok/s decode on Gemma 4 E4B. 7/8 tool-match, 100% arg-match on the 8-case benchmark. 18 HVAC KB entries across 10 brands. Keyword retrieval under 1 ms. Direct follow-up to our Feb 2026 FunctionGemma Hybrid Router (2nd place, DC edition). Gemma 4 E4B is ~15× larger and natively multimodal, so most of the 270M-era workarounds disappeared. I am so happy to introduce Lattices, an open-source research discovery platform that we have developed to visualize scientific literature as a map rather than another ranked list. Lattices retrieves data from OpenAlex, PubMed, zbMATH Open, and arXiv, searching through thousands of research articles across multiple domains. The graph is constructed based on the actual semantic content of the papers: • Every title and abstract is encoded using all-MiniLM-L6-v2. • Cosine similarity finds every paper's closest semantic neighbors. • Papers are first clustered by the era of their publication and then clustered by meaning seeded by K-means. • Cluster names are assigned locally by TF-IDF phrases without any LLM naming the clusters for us. • The newer clusters either link to a semantically similar older cluster or else start their own branch. This results in a chronological research landscape where old themes are closer to the center, new themes spread out, and each paper rotates around its own cluster. Paper similarities are accessible during zoomed-in analysis without overloading the overview. Lattices map semantic similarity and not citation influence, so being connected implies that two papers talk about similar topics, not just that one cites another. The system consists of a Python/FastAPI retrieval and graph pipeline in conjunction with React, TypeScript, Sigma.js, and Graphology interface. It could be executed as a CLI, reusable Python package, local app, and is deployed to lattices.lol via vercel. The hosted version also utilizes ONNX export of MiniLM to maintain efficient semantic inference within a serverless architecture. This was also our team's ( Emmanuel Zhagui-Quito , Nikhil Iyer ) first experience with AI assisted software. We wanted to see if we could turn an idea into a complete, deployed application in under 24 hours. To our surprise this entire venture took under 16! In addition, it taught us a lot about architecture, data structuring, semantic clustering, graph networks, and AI assisted UI design.
